summary:
Sweden's parliament approved new acts on legal gender recognition and on medical procedures performed on genitalia in April 2024, as recorded by a Library of Congress global legal monitor entry of that month.

The Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025. TGEU reports that it simplifies the procedure for changing legal gender but falls short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining, so a person seeking to update legal documents may still be required to satisfy medical conditions.

As adopted in April 2024 by a Riksdag vote of 234 to 94 and effective from 1 July 2025, the minimum age for legal gender change without a gender-dysphoria diagnosis was lowered from 18 to 16, on the basis of a doctor or psychologist statement together with approval from the National Board of Health and Welfare, and with guardian approval required for 16- and 17-year-olds. Genital surgery is limited to those aged 18 and over, and gonad removal to those aged 23 and over absent exceptional reason.

Sweden's main national board decided on 28 January 2017 that transgender people would no longer be classified as mentally ill, the depathologisation step that governs diagnostic status for trans residents.

Transgender identity and expression have been covered by Swedish hate speech legislation since 1 January 2019, and were added to hate crime legislation on 1 July 2018; sexual orientation had been added to hate crime provisions in 2010. Brå, the National Council for Crime Prevention, publishes the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending through report 2024:13, a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences in which police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives.

Facility access is the clearest documented everyday friction. SVT reported in October 2025 that the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their changing rooms.

Access to gender-affirming care for minors is restricted. In March 2021 the Karolinska Institute stopped providing puberty blockers or gender-affirming hormone therapy to children and teenagers under 16, and to 16- to 18-year-olds outside approved clinical trials. On 22 February 2022 the National Board of Health and Welfare stated that puberty blockers should be used only in exceptional cases supported by what it called uncertain science; this is guidance rather than a statutory ban. In 2021 the Board reduced the number of gender-affirming clinics from seven to three. Misinformation that Sweden had banned gender-affirming care for minors nevertheless circulated on social media and was cited by politicians in the United States to justify outright bans. Nationwide Board data released in 2026 showed that trans children prescribed puberty blockers had increased slightly since the 2022 guidance.

Legal gender change was long conditional: until 2013 it required sterilisation and sex reassignment surgery. Those requirements were ruled unconstitutional in January 2013 and removed by the Riksdag in July 2013, and a law passed in March 2018 provided compensation of 225,000 SEK each to roughly 600 to 700 people subjected to forced sterilisation.

Organised opposition to trans rights is a documented feature of the political environment. Anti-gender campaigns mobilise around the pejorative concept of gender ideology, with actors including the far-right Sweden Democrats and the Christian Democrats, who oppose trans-rights legal reforms while framing that opposition as protecting women's rights and Swedish values, alongside gender-critical radical feminist groups such as the Swedish Women's Lobby. Scholars document what they describe as insidious de-democratisation and report growing political violence and intimidation against trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialised activists, including online harassment, threats and public vilification.

Sweden does not criminalise consensual same-sex relations, which have been legal since 1944, and a 2019 Spartacus Gay Travel Index reported by Newsweek ranked Canada, Portugal and Sweden as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations.
tangentialFactors:
A bill covered by the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 would extend protection of victims of conversion practices where those practices are carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure. In November 2025 the Church of Sweden decided that new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, a motion passing with 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council.

The historical record behind current service conditions in the armed forces is traced in an open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy of 4 February 2016 (vol. 13, pp. 119-129), covering LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014.

The Swedish hate speech regime has been criticised as selectively applied. Authorities declined to prosecute a Halmstad imam who called homosexuality a virus in 2015, and the preacher Åke Green was convicted and then acquitted through to the Supreme Court, which held that religious-speech protections under the European Convention barred punishment. The hate speech provision covering sexual orientation was added by Riksdag vote in 2002 and took effect on 1 January 2003.

Anti-gender actors also target knowledge production, labelling gender studies and intersectional feminist scholarship ideological or unscientific, and campaigns extend into education. The Swedish Women's Lobby, founded in 1997 and an umbrella for 57 associations representing over 130,000 women and girls, launched the Women's Platform for Action International in 2025 to promote what it terms sex-based rights.

Sweden's record includes long-running public-health and criminal-law measures unrelated to trans visitors: an equal age of consent at 15 has applied since 1972, homosexuality was declassified as an illness in October 1979, and a 1987 law banning sex in gay saunas and prostitution, enacted to combat HIV, was repealed in 2004.
localsOnly:
The depathologisation decision of 28 January 2017 governs diagnostic status for trans residents rather than visitors, and the compensation scheme for forced sterilisation closed with the March 2018 law paying 225,000 SEK to each of roughly 600 to 700 claimants.

Residents seeking administrative help can turn to RFSL counselling centres in Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö, which assist with contact to authorities and with legal assistance in matters such as asylum and wills. A 1978 state inquiry into the living conditions of gays and lesbians had earlier suggested granting refugee status to persecuted LGBTQ people.

Migrant LGBTQ residents face measurable disadvantage: a 2021 study found worse sexual health, higher avoidance of healthcare, greater exposure to sexual violence and lower satisfaction with their sexual life than other groups.

Domestic political pressure on trans rights is led by the Sweden Democrats and the Christian Democrats and by gender-critical groups including the Swedish Women's Lobby. Documented effects on residents include online harassment, threats and public vilification directed at trans advocates, feminist scholars and racialised activists.

For residents in healthcare, the operative constraints are the Karolinska Institute's March 2021 suspension of puberty blockers and hormones for under-16s and for 16- to 18-year-olds outside trials, the National Board of Health and Welfare's 22 February 2022 guidance, and the reduction of gender-affirming clinics from seven to three in 2021. Board data released in 2026 showed a slight increase in trans children prescribed puberty blockers since that guidance.

Brå's report 2024:13 is the national reference for police-identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives among persons suspected of offences.
outOfScopeNotes:
No visa or entry rules for LGBTQ travellers are sourced for Sweden; the nearest material found is the 1978 state inquiry's refugee-status suggestion, and current asylum criteria are not documented in this inventory.

The date of declassification of transgender status as an illness is given inconsistently in the source coverage, as 2017 in one place and 2009 in another; the 28 January 2017 decision reported by TT/The Local is the item used here, and the 2009 reference remains unresolved.

Whether the pending conversion-practices bill described in the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 has been enacted is not established by the inventory.

The scope of the Medley changing-room restriction beyond that chain, and any parallel policy at other leisure facilities, is not documented.

Brå's dataset records only offences in which police identified an LGBTQI-related motive, so it does not measure unreported or unpolicereported hostility.
